title: Arizona named a top spot for UFO sightings. Here's why
excerpt: A new study showed Arizona having one of the highest amounts of UFO sightings per capita. Here are some of the states most mysterious stories.
content:
Updated Oct. 6, 2026, 6:58 a.m. MT

UFO’s have been a top fascination for people across the globe for centuries; some of the most curious sightings have even been in Arizona. 

Whether you believe it’s all a hoax or one of the world’s greatest mysteries, Arizona has had a fair amount of pretty compelling sightings across the state, many of which have been documented by the FBI.

A report from Casino.ca used more than 160,000 sightings reported to the National UFO Reporting Center between 1974 and 2026 to track the state where UFOs have been most reported per capita.

Arizona reported having some of the highest sightings per capita in the nation, according to the report. Here's why, plus some of Arizona's most unique sightings.

Arizona ranked 6th in US for UFO sightings

According to the Casino.ca report, for every 1,057 residents in Arizona, there has been 1 UFO sighting. When adjusted to Arizona’s estimated population of 7 million, that’s around 6,622 sightings.

These states have highest UFO sightings

Casino.ca reported that these 10 states had the highest number of sightings per capita:

  1. Delaware
  2. New York
  3. Oregon
  4. Washington
  5. Florida
  6. Arizona
  7. Texas
  8. New Mexico
  9. Alaska
  10. California

Arizona's most unexplainable UFOs

Arizona’s most famous UFO sighting was the notorious Phoenix Lights. On March 13, 1997, thousands witnessed a curious V-shaped light show pass through Phoenix’s night sky, sounding alarms for many residents.

The U.S. Air Force attributed the phenomenon to military flares, but skepticism persists to this day. The enduring mystery of the Phoenix Lights has fueled speculation about the possibility of extraterrestrial visitors or clandestine government activities.

However, another information on another compelling case was recently highlighted in the 2026 UFO/UAP document release.

On June 30, 1947, Lt. William G. McGinty, a P-80 aircraft pilot student from Chandler, reported seeing two circular, light-gray objects about eight feet in diameter descending vertically at what he described as “inconceivable speeds” over the Grand Canyon while en route south toward Williams Field Air Force Base in metro Phoenix.

McGinty stated the objects appeared to be heading straight down toward an area roughly 25 miles south of the South Rim before he instinctively turned his aircraft away from them while continuing south toward Williams Field Air Force Base. He noted that one object followed the other only seconds apart.

What makes the incident notable is that the same Grand Canyon account appears repeatedly across three separate FBI sections, including interview summaries, agent review notes and serial reports, suggesting federal investigators considered the sighting significant enough to document and circulate internally.

Days later, on July 8, 1947, agents referenced additional reports of similarly fast-moving unidentified objects and an FBI agent obtained photographs of unidentified aerial objects from the managing editor of The Arizona Republic.

The photographs had been taken by William Rhodes at sunset on July 7, 1947, after the objects reportedly flew at “inconceivable speeds” while making three circles near Rhodes’ home in Phoenix. Using a size-620 box camera, Rhodes captured one image as the object passed in front of him and another as it turned toward him.
